content: The Tai Chi Classics are a collection of manuscripts and commentaries that serve as authoritative guides for the proper study and practice of tai chi chuan. These texts, which differ between schools, are traditionally written in classical Chinese and are utilized by modern schools tracing their lineage to the Chen family or, through them, to the Yang family. While many of these writings are attributed to legendary figures and claimed to be of great antiquity, modern research has not been able to date any of them earlier than the late 19th century. Below are some of the most notable works considered part of the Tai Chi Classics: 1. T'ai Chi Ch'uan Classic (T'ai Chi Ch'uan Ching 太極拳經): This text is attributed to Chang San-feng (Zhang Sanfeng), the legendary founder of tai chi chuan, and is claimed to date back to the 12th-14th century. 2. Salt Shop Manual (鹽店譜): This contains the T'ai Chi Ch'uan Treatise (T'ai Chi Ch'uan Lun 太極拳論), which is attributed to the legendary Wang Tsung-yueh (Wang Zongyue). The text was reportedly discovered in the back room of a Beijing salt shop by Wu Yu-hsiang's brother, Wu Ch'eng-ch'ing (Wu Chengqing). 3. Miscellaneous Texts: These include works such as the Song of Thirteen Postures, Mental Elucidation of the Practice of T'ai Chi Ch'uan, and the Song of Sparring, which have been passed down through the Yang and Wu families. 4. Texts by Wu Yu-hsiang (武禹襄): Wu Yu-hsiang (1812–1880), a key figure in the Wu/Hao style of Tai Chi Chuan, and his relatives contributed significant writings to the tradition. 5. Forty Chapters: This is a collection of writings preserved within the Yang and Wu families. 6. T'ai Chi Ch'uan Illustrated (太極拳圖說): Published in 1919 by Chen Xin (陳鑫, 1849–1929), an important scholar from the Chen family, this work provides a detailed visual and textual explanation of tai chi chuan. 7. The Study of T'ai Chi Ch'uan (太極拳學): First published in 1924 by Sun Lu-t'ang (孫祿堂, 1861–1932), the founder of the fifth and final classical style of tai chi chuan, this book is a significant contribution to the field. 8. Complete Principles and Applications of T'ai Chi Ch'uan: Published in 1934 by Yang Ch'eng-fu (楊澄甫, 1883–1936), this work is considered authoritative in schools influenced by Yang's students and descendants. It includes the famous Ten Essential Points of Taijiquan Theory, authored by Yang Ch'eng-fu. 9. Wu Family T'ai Chi Ch'uan (吳家太極拳): Wu Kung-tsao (吳公藻, 1902–1983) provided original texts and commentary on the Forty Chapters in this book. Wu's grandfather, Wu Ch'uan-yu (吳全佑, 1834–1902), inherited the Forty Chapters from Yang Pan-hou (楊班侯, 1837–1890). The book was first published in Changsha in 1935. When it was republished in Hong Kong in 1980, the renowned wuxia author Jin Yong contributed a postscript, highlighting the influence of ancient Chinese philosophers such as Lao Tzu and Chuang Tzu on modern Chinese martial arts. Collections, Translations, and Studies Several modern scholars and practitioners have translated and studied the Tai Chi Classics, producing works that make these texts accessible to a broader audience. Notable examples include: Barbara Davis, The Taijiquan Classics: An Annotated Translation (2004) Jou Tsung-hwa, The Tao of T'ai Chi Ch'uan (1980) T.T. Liang, T'ai Chi Ch'uan for Health and Self-Defense: Philosophy and Practice (1977) Benjamin Lo, Martin Inn, Robert Amacker, and Susan Foe, The Essence of T'ai Chi Ch'uan: The Literary Tradition (1979) Douglas Wile, Lost T'ai-chi Classics from the Late Ch'ing Dynasty (1996)
